title: Incidents, postmortems and chaos engineering
problem: The pager fires at 3 a.m., three engineers debug the same thing in three chats, nobody updates customers, and the same outage returns next quarter.
summary: Incident response runs an outage with severity levels, an incident commander who delegates operations and communications, a live timeline and a status page, then learns from it with a blameless postmortem whose action items buy back the error budget.
catTip: When the fish tank overflows, one cat commands, one cat mops and one cat tells the humans. Afterwards nobody blames the cat who knocked the pump; we ask why the pump could be knocked. Then we practise knocking it on purpose.

recall.q: Who runs an incident and what does each role own?
recall.a: The incident commander owns the overall picture and every role not delegated; the operations lead owns the fix; the communications lead owns updates to the status page and stakeholders. The live incident document holds the timeline, which becomes the postmortem.

guide.breaks: Without roles and a timeline, several people fix the same thing while nobody talks to customers, and without a blameless postmortem the organisation hides causes and repeats the outage.
guide.tradeoffs: Formal roles, status cadences, postmortem reviews and game days cost engineering time on every incident and every quarter, and averages such as MTTR are too noisy to prove the investment is paying off.
guide.explainSimply: An incident is run like an emergency room: triage decides how serious it is, one person leads and does not also operate, one person keeps the chart and one talks to the family. Afterwards the team reviews the chart without blaming anyone and fixes what let the mistake happen. Then they rehearse, so that the next real emergency is not the first time.
guide.hint: Think about the three jobs that must happen at once during an outage and who holds the ones nobody has taken.

meow: Page, meow. Commander, mopper, talker. Timeline, status page, blameless postmortem. Then we break it on purpose, gently.

quiz.prompt: During a SEV-1, the engineer fixing the database also keeps replying to executives and updating the status page. According to the incident command model, what is wrong?
options: Nothing; the person closest to the problem knows the most and should communicate it
Operations and communications are held by one person, so neither is done well and nobody holds the overall picture
Executives should not be told about an incident until the postmortem is written
Status page updates should wait until the root cause is known
quiz.explanation: The model separates the incident commander, the operations lead and the communications lead precisely so that fixing and informing do not compete for one person's attention. The last option is the believable error: status pages are updated on a cadence with what is known so far, never held back for a root cause.

quiz.prompt: Why does Google's analysis warn against using MTTR to judge whether reliability work is paying off?
options: Because MTTR only counts incidents that monitoring detected
Because incident durations vary so widely and there are so few of them that the mean swings by chance, hiding or inventing improvements
Because MTTR double-counts incidents that have more than one root cause
Because MTTR is measured in minutes while SLOs are measured in percentages
quiz.explanation: Davidovič's Monte Carlo simulations show that heavy-tailed durations and small samples make the mean unreliable for decisions or trends. The first option is the plausible distractor, but detection method is a problem for MTTD's definition, not the statistical flaw in averaging recovery times.

cards.q: Name the five triggers the SRE book lists for writing a postmortem.
cards.a: User-visible downtime or degradation beyond a threshold; data loss of any kind; on-call intervention such as a rollback or traffic reroute; a resolution time above a threshold; a monitoring failure, which usually means someone found the incident by hand.

cards.q: A postmortem concludes that the engineer should have been more careful. What is wrong, and what replaces it?
cards.a: It blames a person rather than the system, so the next person in the same situation will fail the same way and people will hide details next time. Replace it with the conditions that made the mistake possible and action items with owners: a guard rail, a test, a runbook step.

glossary.note: Average time from a fault starting to the alert; useful per incident, noisy as a quarterly average.
Average time from alert (or fault) to service restored; heavy-tailed durations and small samples make it a poor trend metric.
The emergency-management structure firefighters created in 1968, with a single commander delegating roles; Google's incident response is adapted from it.

sources.title: Google SRE Book, ch. 14 "Managing Incidents"
sources.supports: the three conditions for declaring an incident; incident command, operational work and communication roles; the commander holds undelegated roles; live incident state document, recognised command post, clear live handoff

sources.title: Google SRE Book, ch. 15 "Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure"
sources.supports: blameless postmortems; the five postmortem triggers; an unreviewed postmortem might as well never have existed

sources.title: Google SRE Book, Appendix D "Example Postmortem"
sources.supports: the template sections: summary, impact, root causes, trigger, resolution, detection, action items with type and owner, lessons learned, timeline

sources.title: Google SRE Book, ch. 11 "Being On-Call"
sources.supports: the 50% cap on operational work and 25% on-call cap; at most two incidents per 12-hour shift; 5-minute and 30-minute response-time expectations

sources.title: Google SRE Book, ch. 6 "Monitoring Distributed Systems"
sources.supports: every page should be actionable and urgent; page on symptoms rather than causes

sources.title: Google SRE Book, ch. 3 "Embracing Risk"
sources.supports: releases are halted while the error budget is exhausted

sources.title: Google SRE Workbook, ch. 9 "Incident Response"

sources.title: Google SRE Workbook, ch. 10 "Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure"
